- Example: machine code / assembly language (1)
scheme.model_answer: A language whose instructions correspond directly to the processor's instruction set, so it is close to the hardware — for example assembly language.

questions.title: Define a high-level language

- Example: Python, Java, C#, C++, Pascal, JavaScript, SQL (1)

questions.title: Two differences
questions.text: Give **two** differences between high-level and low-level languages.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each), both sides stated or implied: portable vs machine-dependent; easy vs hard to read / write / debug; shorter vs longer development time; compiler / interpreter vs assembler / no translation; indirect vs direct hardware control; slower / more memory vs faster / less memory; one-to-many vs one-to-one; no hardware knowledge needed vs must know the processor

questions.text: Explain the difference between the **one-to-one** relationship of assembly language and the **one-to-many** relationship of high-level languages with machine code.

- One-to-one: each assembly instruction translates into exactly one machine-code instruction (1)
- One-to-many: one high-level statement translates into several / many machine-code instructions (1)
scheme.model_answer: Each assembly instruction becomes exactly one machine-code instruction, whereas a single high-level statement such as total = a + b becomes several machine-code instructions.

questions.title: Imperative vs declarative
questions.text: Write **two** differences between declarative and imperative programming languages.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): what vs how; execution order not clearly delineated vs clearly defined sequence of instructions; logic / query / functional vs procedural / object-oriented; little or no changing state vs variables changed by assignment

questions.title: Choosing a language level
questions.text:
A company makes fitness trackers. The tracker has a tiny processor and 64 KB of memory. The company also needs a phone app, for Android and iPhone, that shows the user's data.

Discuss which type of language (high-level or low-level) is more suitable for **each** program.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Tracker (max 2): low-level / assembly (1) — small memory, fast code, direct control of sensors / battery (1)
Phone app (max 2): high-level (1) — portable to Android and iPhone / faster development / easier to maintain / graphical interface libraries (1)
scheme.model_answer: The tracker program should be written in a low-level language such as assembly, because it must fit into 64 KB and run efficiently on the small processor while controlling the sensors directly. The phone app should be written in a high-level language, because it can be developed faster, uses libraries for the user interface and can be translated to run on both Android and iPhone.

questions.title: Compare high-level and low-level
questions.text: Compare high-level and low-level programming languages. Include examples of each type and situations in which each would be used.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Comparison points (max 4), each with both sides: readability / ease; portability; translation (compiler / interpreter vs assembler / none); hardware control; speed / memory; development time; one-to-many vs one-to-one
Examples (1): correct example of each (e.g. Python and assembly)
Situations (1): appropriate use of each (e.g. apps vs device drivers / embedded systems)
scheme.model_answer: High-level languages such as Python use English-like keywords, so they are easier to read, write and debug than low-level languages such as assembly, which use mnemonics. High-level programs are portable, whereas low-level programs are written for one processor. High-level code is translated by a compiler or interpreter, and each statement becomes many machine instructions; assembly is translated one-to-one by an assembler. Low-level languages give direct control of registers and memory and produce faster, smaller programs. High-level languages are used for applications and websites, while low-level languages are used for device drivers and embedded systems with little memory.

summary: How programming languages are classified into low-level (machine code, assembly) and high-level languages, how they compare, when each is used, language generations, and the difference between imperative and declarative languages.

blocks.content: A **programming language** is a formal language for writing instructions that a computer can carry out. Languages are classified by **how close they are to the hardware** (low-level) or **to human language** (high-level).

flowchart LR
  PL[Programming languages] --> LL[Low-level]
  PL --> HL[High-level]
  LL --> MC[Machine code — 1st generation]
  LL --> AS[Assembly language — 2nd generation]
  HL --> IM[Imperative: Python, C, Java, Pascal]
  HL --> DE[Declarative: SQL, Prolog, Haskell]
blocks.caption: Classification of programming languages

blocks.content: A language that is **close to the machine's hardware** — its instructions correspond directly to the processor's **instruction set**. It is **machine-dependent** (written for one type of processor). Includes **machine code** and **assembly language**.

A language that is **close to human language and mathematical notation**, uses **English-like keywords** (`if`, `while`, `print`) and is **machine-independent** (portable). One statement usually becomes **many** machine-code instructions. Examples: Python, Java, C#, C++, Pascal, JavaScript.

Instructions written in **binary** (or hexadecimal) that the **CPU can execute directly**, without translation. Each instruction has an **opcode** (the operation) and an **operand** (the data or address).

A low-level language that uses short **mnemonics** (`LDA`, `ADD`, `STA`, `JMP`) and **labels** instead of binary codes. Each assembly instruction usually translates into **exactly one** machine-code instruction (**one-to-one**). It is translated by an **assembler**.

blocks.title: The same task at three levels — add two numbers and store the result

blocks.content:
LDA #0        ; accumulator ← 0
        STA count
LOOP:   LDA count
        ADD #1        ; count ← count + 1
        STA count
        CMP #10
        BNE LOOP      ; repeat until count = 10
        HLT

items.title: Features of high-level languages
items.content:
- **English-like keywords** and mathematical symbols (`if total > 100:`).
- **Data structures** (arrays, records, lists) and **control structures** (selection, loops, functions).
- **Portable** — the same source code runs on different processors after translation.
- Translated by a **compiler** or **interpreter**; one statement → many machine instructions (**one-to-many**).
- Large **libraries** of ready-made functions.

items.title: Language generations
items.content:
- **1GL** — machine code (binary).
- **2GL** — assembly language (mnemonics).
- **3GL** — high-level procedural / object-oriented languages: C, Pascal, Python, Java.
- **4GL** — closer to human language, often for a specific purpose: **SQL**, report generators.
- **5GL** — describe the problem with constraints / logic; the system solves it: **Prolog** (AI).

items.title: When to use a high-level language
items.content:
- Most **applications**: business software, websites, mobile apps, games.
- When **development speed**, readability and **maintenance** by a team matter.
- When the program must run on **different types of computers**.

items.title: When to use a low-level language
items.content:
- **Device drivers** and parts of the **operating system** that control hardware directly.
- **Embedded systems** with very little memory and slow processors (washing machine, microwave, sensor).
- **Time-critical** code that must run as fast as possible (real-time control, some game engines).
- When a program must fit into a **very small amount of memory** (ROM).

blocks.title: Choose the language
blocks.content:
- *A washing-machine controller with 2 KB of ROM* → **assembly** (small, fast, direct control of the motor and sensors).
- *A school timetable app for Android and iPhone* → **high-level** (portable, quick to develop, easy to maintain).
- *A driver for a new graphics card* → **low-level** (direct access to the hardware registers).
High-level languages can also be classified by **paradigm** — the style in which the program describes a problem.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Give two differences between high-level and low-level languages. [2]**
A high-level language is **portable / machine-independent**, whereas a low-level language is written for **one type of processor** (1). Low-level code gives **direct control of the hardware** and runs **faster / uses less memory**, whereas high-level code is **easier to write and debug** (1).

**Q: Explain why assembly language might be used to write the program for a microwave oven. [2]**
The microwave has a **small amount of memory**, and assembly produces **compact, fast code** (1); it also gives **direct control** of the hardware such as the timer and the magnetron (1).

**Q: State what is meant by a one-to-one relationship between assembly language and machine code. [1]**
Each assembly-language **instruction translates into exactly one** machine-code instruction.

**Q: Write two differences between declarative and imperative programming. [2]**
Declarative focuses on **what** the program should achieve, whereas imperative focuses on **how** (1). An imperative program is a **clearly defined sequence of instructions**, whereas in a declarative program the execution order is **not clearly delineated** (1).

- Saying low-level languages are "easier for the computer to understand" — only **machine code** is executed directly; **assembly must be assembled**.
- Saying high-level programs "run faster" — usually they run **slower** than well-written low-level code.
- Writing "high-level is easy" without a comparison — use **whereas** and state both sides.
- Calling assembly language "binary" — it uses **mnemonics**.
- Thinking SQL and Prolog are low-level — they are **high-level declarative** languages.
